interest: This file offers a unique view into how the radio spectrum became an arena of pre–World War II geopolitical and technical friction between the United States and Imperial Japan. It illuminates interdepartmental coordination among the State, War, and Navy Departments and the FCC, especially regarding international telecommunications law, Bern Bureau priority disputes, and diplomatic sensitivities surrounding Manchukuo. Crucially, the documents capture the transition from routine technical frequency coordination to early electronic warfare, documenting civilian listener reports and diplomatic inquiries into suspected deliberate Japanese jamming of American shortwave news broadcasts.
overview: This file documents extensive diplomatic, technical, and interdepartmental communications between the United States and Japan from January 1930 to October 1939 regarding radio frequency interference across transpacific circuits. The correspondence—involving the Department of State, War Department, Navy Department, Federal Radio Commission/Federal Communications Commission, U.S. diplomatic missions in East Asia, and commercial entities like RCA and Press Wireless—details recurring interference caused by Japanese commercial, naval, and colonial stations to U.S. naval reception, Army transpacific circuits, maritime distress channels, amateur bands, and commercial radiotelegraphy. Major subjects include technical negotiations over frequency shifts, transmitter modernizations, and harmonic suppression; interdepartmental deliberations over an aborted bilateral technical conference in Tokyo; legal disputes over frequency notification priorities under Bern Bureau and Madrid Convention regulations; Japanese commercial telegraph routing policies; and late-1930s diplomatic investigations into alleged intentional Japanese jamming of American shortwave news broadcasts from station W6XBE/KGEI.
